guide.title: Repository-authored design example — read this as a consistency-boundary design, not as a question of whether the database or the queue should be written first.
guide.problem: Service A must update its own record in its local database and ask Service B to create another one. The local database commit and broker publish are two independent writes, so either ordering leaves a crash window in which one succeeds and the other does not; this is a repository-authored design example, not a verified production deployment.
guide.core_idea: Commit the business change and an outbox event in the same local database transaction. A relay publishes that durable event later and may record PUBLISHED only as its observation of the broker publication boundary; Service B processes duplicates safely by recording the event ID and its business update in one local database transaction.
guide.outcome: The design removes the lost-event window at the local database boundary without a distributed transaction. It deliberately provides at-least-once delivery, then turns duplicates into harmless retries and models payment, inventory and shipping as explicit order-state transitions with compensating actions. An asynchronous API returns a durable pending status resource; unknown provider outcomes, expiry, terminal failure, reconciliation and authorized replay remain explicit recovery paths.
takeaways: No ordering of two independent writes makes a dual write atomic. Database-first can lose the notification; broker-first can expose an event for a business change that never commits. Outbox closes only the same local database's intent boundary.

The relay may publish twice. PUBLISHED is a relay observation of the broker boundary, not proof that a consumer or business effect completed; a crash after broker acknowledgement but before marking the row published makes duplicate delivery unavoidable, so consumers must be idempotent.

Inbox deduplication and the consumer's business update belong in the same local database transaction. A durable business-key constraint protects intent separately; checking an event ID before that transaction only creates another check-then-act race.
Outbox solves transport reliability, not business sequencing. A Saga or state machine defines which event may move an order from PAYMENT_PENDING to PAID, RESERVED, SHIPPED or a compensating state.

Return the state that is already durable. An asynchronous checkout should normally return an order ID and a status resource with pending or unknown states, expiry, terminal failure and authorization rules, not claim that the workflow has finished.
review_lenses: Atomicity: identify every place that writes a local database and calls an external system in one logical operation; state exactly which boundary is atomic.
Duplicate safety: define the stable event ID, business uniqueness key, provider idempotency scope and local transaction boundary at every consumer.
Recovery: specify lease expiry and reclaim, stale or gap events, unknown provider outcomes, terminal failure, reconciliation and authorized redrive with an owner.

Operations: measure outbox oldest age, claim expiry, publish/mark mismatch, Inbox and DLQ age, pending/unknown age and reconciliation debt; attach thresholds, runbooks and opaque non-sensitive trace IDs. For the illustrative SKIP LOCKED claim, state the MySQL 8.4/InnoDB and transaction-isolation assumptions, because skipped rows are a queue-like view rather than a general correctness read. The reliability claim is falsified when the relay claim model — lease, row state or advisory lock — has no reclaim path; when a duplicate can arrive after the Inbox retention window without a durable business key behind it; when the external provider is not idempotent and the sample still shows a bare retry instead of status inquiry and reconciliation; when legal or tenant retention requires payload deletion the event archive cannot honour; or when a property test under crash and retry injection cannot show exactly one local transition and one durable intent per accepted command.
